R2 storage enforcement no longer holds a pooled DB connection and open transaction across Cloudflare calls (issue #666).

- The per-owner `r2_enforcement_lock` (a `pg_advisory_xact_lock` whose transaction -- and pooled Neon connection -- stayed open for the whole critical section, including every Cloudflare token-policy call) is replaced by `r2_enforcement_lease`: a DB lease row (`r2_enforcement_leases`, migration 033) acquired, renewed, and released in short single-statement transactions, with client-side poll-waiting. No connection is held while the lease is held, and a dropped connection now degrades into a bounded, observable takeover-after-expiry instead of a silent unlock.

- The lease is renewed (and ownership proven) before each key's Cloudflare call, so a holder that stalls past the lease expiry aborts at the next key boundary instead of interleaving writes with the holder that took over. The sweep skips (and counts) owners whose lease is contended or lost; the grant/recheck endpoints answer a structured, retryable 503 (`enforcement_busy` / `enforcement_interrupted`); the suspend/unsuspend storage steps record a contended or taken-over lease in the per-step report (the operator re-runs, as with any other partial step failure).

- Key-policy transitions now record write-ahead markers: `enforced_access = 'pending'` (quota sweep/grants/recheck) and `suspension_access = 'pending_read'` / `'pending_disabled'` (suspension) are written before the Cloudflare call and settled after it, so a crash between the two leaves the key recorded as in-flight -- re-asserted by the next enforcement pass -- rather than recorded as untouched while its live token policy silently diverges. Consumers treat a pending marker conservatively (as read-only/enforced).
